Custom routing metric for links

A link's routing metric could only be one of four presets (Prefer,
Normal, Avoid, Backup only). Links now also get a Custom option, closer
to how real networks tune IGP metrics:

- Multiplier mode scales the distance cost, (km + 60) × 0.1 to 100.
- Cost mode sets an exact cost, 1 to 65535 like an OSPF metric.

The preset buttons stay plain. Picking Custom explains how a link's cost
is worked out and lists what each preset comes to on that link. Choosing
Custom starts from the current preset and switching modes keeps the
effective cost, so nothing moves until the player changes the value.
Like the presets, it applies to every link between the two cities.

The cost formula lives in one helper, linkW(), used by compute() and the
traceroute paths. Custom links store mk/mv, which sanitize() repairs and
clamps; old saves load unchanged. The link panel skips its daily
re-render while the number field has focus, and Enter applies the value.

Tests cover routing equivalence with the presets, rerouting by cost,
mode switching, input clamping, saves, and the panel at desktop and
phone width. French, Italian and Portuguese for the new strings.

Pinned attack flows are routed even when RouteScript moves every other exit off their rank

The rank loop skips ranks no list uses (RSET), but flows pinned to an entry
port route at the port's plain rank. With 'prepend transit' or 'prefer transit'
moving every transit to 2.9/4.4, rank 3 was skipped and the flood vanished.
Fixes tests/routing-reference.test.js, which failed on v2.

Routing: a flow scans only the exits on its own island

The big fixture is a dozen islands (POPs no backbone joins). Each flow scanned every exit in its
rank's list and threw away the unreachable ones, two thirds of the scan. Lists are now split per
island once per compute; with one island nothing changes. Same exits, same order, same result
(routing-reference gains a network-of-islands case).

Routing: remember each list's first exit group per source city while its exits have room

Most flows from one city ask the same rank list for the same nearest group of exits. Exits only
fill up while routing, so while every exit in that group still has room the scan would find it
again; it is reused instead. Networks with identical exit lists share one list, so the memory
serves them all. Same groups, same order, same result (routing-reference and speed tests).
Every city has its country code; the 2x border toll stays an African thing

Sales trial: run the pass with the offer first, and skip the other when it cannot change the answer

With events booked ahead the trial routed the network twice: without the offer (who is happy now)
and with it. compute() only reads the previous result for scenic circuits, so without those the
order of the two passes does not matter. With the offer first, a failing offer or one nobody is
unhappy with needs no second pass. The same offers are signed (tests/sales-trial.test.js checks
over 100 seeded offers against the original trial, scenic or not).

Billing: a recompute after the day tick no longer counts today's 95th-percentile sample twice

dayTick() routes the day, then appends today's transit use to t.hist. Every
compute() after that (any click, the intern, the sales trial) took the last 29
entries of t.hist, which now end on today, and added today's use again: today
counted twice and the 30th day back dropped out. So compute() gave a different
transit bill the second time after each day. p95() now leaves today's sample out
once S.hist says the day has been recorded.

This was the only part of compute() that was not a pure function of S. The rest
of the drift round 1 saw (R right after dayTick vs. a fresh compute) is dayTick
itself changing S after its compute (customers churning, events ending), which
is intended: the next day routes the new state. Scenic circuits' hysteresis is
documented, with a test that two calls converge.

Each attack is again one entry port at the victim (a.entry): upstream clean-pipe,
Flowspec on the victim's router, IX blackholing, a sacrificial PNI and RouteScript
filter it in that order (ddosMitigation), then scrubbing; what leaks is junk at the

Submarine upgrades that change nothing on a cable can't be bought (#198)

long-haul modes of the coherent optics. On many cable lengths (all of
the Atlantic, and about 17,000-18,500 km like Atlanta to Sydney) neither
changes what any optic carries, yet both could be bought.

subHelps() compares every optic's rate with and without the upgrade,
counting an upgrade that only helps together with the other one. The
link panel disables Install with a note, ACT.subUpgrade refuses, and
the cable order screen disables the toggle and only quotes and charges
picks that still help on the chosen design.

Map: a link's curve only measures the cities that could be in its way

A carrier's own transit port takes its traffic, with a Carry here switch for other POPs

Transit ports at a POP shared load by free capacity whatever the traffic
was for, so Level Tree's own traffic went out of a Tell-Ya port about
half the time. Traffic bound for a carrier, or for a network that buys
transit from it, now goes out of that carrier's port at the same POP
first (the shorter AS path). Each such port is still an ordinary transit
exit, so POPs without one use it when nothing nearer has room.

A new switch on each transit port, Carry here, pulls that traffic from
every POP across your network to this port. The default, Nearest port,
keeps using the closest transit port from POPs that have no port of the
carrier. The switch only shows when another carrier's port could take
the traffic instead.

Prefer-marked ports, Backup only, RouteScript and Auto-TE keep their say,
and any Prefer-marked transit port switches the rule off. Traceroute
follows the same rule and says why it picked an exit. The setting is
repaired in sanitize(); old saves load with it off.
